Unit 3 · World War I · Blue Valley Academy

Understanding Trench Warfare

19th Century Tactics, 20th Century Technology

1915 to 1918

When WWI began both sides expected a short war of movement. By the winter of 1914 the armies were stuck, they dug in, and the line of trenches ran more than four hundred miles from the English Channel to Switzerland. Neither side could go around this line, so for three years they tried to go through it.

Generals still trained officers to win battles the way Napoleon won them: mass your men, charge the enemy line, break it. That tactic met machine guns, barbed wire and industrial artillery. The result was stalemate and roughly nine million dead soldiers.

01What the Ground Looked Like

Soldiers of A Company, 11th Battalion, the Cheshire Regiment hold a captured German trench at Ovillers la Boisselle on the Somme, July 1916. One man keeps sentry while the rest sleep. Because they took this trench from the Germans, he is watching over what used to be the back wall, standing on a fire step his unit cut into the wrong side. John Warwick Brooke, Imperial War Museums Q 3990
Look for: how many men are asleep, and what the one awake is doing
An explosion near trenches dug into the grounds of Fort de la Pompelle, near Reims, France. San Diego Air and Space Museum
Look for: the sandbags and the wire posts
Soldiers in the trenches write letters home. Life in the trenches was summed up by a phrase that became well known: months of boredom punctuated by moments of extreme terror. Netherlands Nationaal Archief
Look for: how narrow the world is
Australian field artillery troops walk a duckboard track across a shattered battlefield in Chateau Wood, near Hooge, Belgium, October 29, 1917, during the Battle of Passchendaele. Shelling destroyed the drainage of the low ground, and the mud that followed was deep enough to drown wounded men. Standing in it for days caused trench foot, a condition in which the feet essentially rot. James Francis Hurley, State Library of New South Wales
Look for: what happened to the forest
Massive craters from detonation of underground mines
Multiple generations of trenches from years of war
Thousands of craters from artillery shells and mortars
The same ground from the air. Almost nothing here is natural. San Diego Air and Space Museum Archive
Look for: how little ground changed hands
